text: Drop Mount Everest into the ocean, and its peak would still be a mile underwater.
So what's down there? Let's sink.
The ocean holds ninety-nine percent of Earth's living space. As one bathtub, it would be eleven hundred kilometres on each side.
A hundred metres. Blue whales hunt here, in the last of the sunlight.
Two hundred and ten. USS Triton's diving depth, the first submarine to circle the world underwater, in 1960.
Two hundred and fifty-three. The deepest free dive ever, on one breath. The pressure is twenty-six times the surface. Enough to crush most human lungs.
So how do whales survive? Blue whales reach five hundred metres. Sperm whales go far deeper, hunting giant squid.
Seven hundred and thirty. Attack submarines turn back here. Any deeper, and the hull could implode.
Hang the Burj Khalifa upside down from the surface, and its tip stops about here.
And at one thousand metres, the sunlight runs out completely. Below this line, it's night forever. And things still live there. Part two.
